problem: This paper investigates how one hyperparameter, kernel bandwidth, shapes the performance of quantum kernels.
gap: Earlier studies largely overlooked hyperparameters and reported that quantum kernel performance falls as qubits increase.
method: The authors identify the parameter that controls bandwidth and test several quantum kernels on classical datasets through large numerical studies, relating the behaviour to classical kernels.
results: Models moved from underfitting at large bandwidth to overfitting at small bandwidth, with the best generalisation in between. Optimising bandwidth reduced the exponential decay of kernel values, so performance improved with qubit count and became competitive with leading classical methods.
limits: The results come from numerical simulation, so finite sampling and device noise on hardware may reduce the benefit. Bandwidth also adds another setting that must be tuned.
mm: Numerical experiments, multiple kernels and classical datasets
f: Tuned bandwidth counters kernel decay; performance competitive with classical

problem: This experiment tests whether a quantum kernel classifier can handle real high-dimensional data on noisy hardware.
gap: Earlier demonstrations were small and used synthetic datasets, leaving the practical difficulties of scaling on noisy devices largely unaddressed.
method: On Google's Sycamore processor, 17 qubits were used to label 67-dimensional cosmology data without compressing it. They designed a circuit that keeps kernel magnitudes from vanishing and applied error mitigation tailored to kernels.
results: Test-set classification accuracy was comparable to noiseless simulation, showing that careful circuit design and mitigation can preserve useful kernels on real hardware.
limits: The demonstration concerns a single cosmology dataset and depends on a tailored circuit. Accuracy comparable to simulation does not by itself show an advantage over classical methods.
f: Test accuracy comparable to noiseless simulation
l: One dataset; no classical advantage shown

problem: This paper asks whether the advantage of quantum kernels survives the noise and limited measurements of near-term machines.
gap: Earlier results showing lower generalisation error for quantum kernels were mostly established in an ideal setting that ignored these hardware issues.
method: The authors analyse kernels theoretically while including system noise and sampling error, propose a remedy based on indefinite kernel learning, and check their results with numerical simulations.
results: The advantage vanishes for large datasets, few measurements and large system noise. The indefinite kernel learning method is offered as a way of preserving the benefit, and the simulations agree with the theory.
limits: The evidence is theoretical and simulated rather than taken from hardware, and the remedy has not been shown here on practical datasets such as medical records.
technique: Noisy quantum kernel theory; indefinite kernel learning
f: Advantage vanishes with large data, few shots and large noise
l: No hardware; not tested on practical data

problem: This review covers variational quantum algorithms (VQAs), which train a parametrised circuit with a classical optimiser.
gap: Fault-tolerant machines are unlikely to arrive soon, and current devices are limited in qubit number and in circuit depth because of noise. A broad account of how to work within these limits was needed.
method: The authors give an overview of the field, its applications and the strategies proposed for overcoming its main difficulties.
results: VQAs have been proposed for nearly every envisioned quantum application and are presented as the leading near-term strategy. Trainability, accuracy and efficiency remain the main challenges.
limits: As a review it offers no new empirical test, and its optimism about advantage is a prospect that has still to be demonstrated in practical applications.
mm: Survey of design, training and applications
f: VQAs are a leading near-term strategy; trainability and accuracy remain challenges
l: No new tests; advantage still a prospect

problem: This review summarises what can be attempted on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computers before error correction becomes available.
gap: Fully fault-tolerant machines need millions of good qubits and may take decades, whereas noisy devices with limited coherence already exist. A thorough account of their algorithms was therefore useful.
method: The authors summarise NISQ paradigms and algorithms across physics, machine learning, chemistry and combinatorial optimisation, along with benchmarking and software tools.
results: The review explains the shared structure of these algorithms along with their limitations and advantages. It gives readers a common map of the field rather than a single new performance result.
limits: Because the review covers many fields, machine learning receives only part of its attention, and individual claims still require independent benchmarking on specific problems.
mm: Survey of paradigms, benchmarks and software tools
f: Common structure, limits and advantages of NISQ algorithms mapped
l: Broad coverage; ML is only one part

problem: This paper studies how the way data is encoded determines what functions a parametrised quantum circuit can represent.
gap: Although such circuits had been widely applied, many of their basic theoretical properties as function approximators remained unknown.
method: The authors analyse quantum models mathematically by expressing their outputs through a partial Fourier series over the inputs.
results: The available frequencies are set by the data-encoding gates, and repeating simple encoding gates gives access to a richer spectrum. With a sufficiently rich spectrum, some of these models are universal function approximators.
limits: Being able to represent a function does not guarantee that a model can be trained or that it generalises well. The analysis also concerns expressive power rather than performance on real datasets.
f: Encoding gates set accessible frequencies; repetition enriches spectrum
l: Says nothing about trainability or real data

problem: This foundational paper asks how much classification power a very small quantum circuit can provide.
gap: One qubit seems too limited for classifying complex data, because it holds only a simple superposition and its gates are single rotations.
method: The authors load the data repeatedly, alternating re-uploading steps with single-qubit processing units and using a classical subroutine for optimisation. They also extend the design to several qubits and benchmark it on varied examples.
results: A single qubit assisted in this way forms a universal quantum classifier. Multi-dimensional inputs and several output classes can be handled, and adding entanglement across qubits improves efficiency.
limits: The benchmarks are described as examples of complex data rather than a clinical task, and the abstract does not assess hardware noise. Practical medical value therefore remains open.
mm: Single- and multi-qubit circuits on benchmark examples
f: One qubit with re-uploading forms a universal classifier
l: Hardware noise and clinical data not assessed

problem: This paper looks for a training strategy that makes parametrised quantum circuits easier to optimise on near-term devices.
gap: The difficult cost landscapes of these circuits, including barren plateaus, make standard full-circuit training unreliable.
method: In layerwise learning the circuit depth is increased gradually during optimisation, and only a subset of parameters is updated in each step. The method was tested on a handwritten digit classification task with sampling noise considered.
results: It reached an 8% lower generalisation error on average than standard schemes for circuits of the same size. The share of runs reaching lower test errors was up to 40% larger.
limits: The evidence comes from one image task, and the approach reduces the risk of plateaus rather than removing it for all circuits and datasets.
mm: Handwritten digit classification with sampling noise
f: 8% lower generalisation error; up to 40% more runs reach lower error
l: One image task; plateau risk reduced, not removed

problem: This paper compares the expressibility and trainability of quantum neural networks (QNNs) with those of classical networks.
gap: The near-term benefits of QML were unclear, and expressibility and trainability of quantum models both needed further study.
method: Using information geometry, the authors define an effective dimension based on the Fisher information, prove a generalisation bound, and connect the Fisher spectrum to barren plateaus. Results were also verified on real quantum hardware.
results: Well-designed QNNs reached a significantly higher effective dimension than comparable classical networks. Certain QNNs also resisted barren plateaus and trained faster, owing to a more evenly spread Fisher spectrum.
limits: The benefit is stated for well-designed networks, not QNNs in general, and higher effective dimension does not automatically produce better accuracy on practical data.
mm: Information geometry; verification on real hardware
f: Well-designed QNNs show higher effective dimension and faster training
l: Only for well-designed QNNs; accuracy on real data not ensured

problem: This paper asks how the choice of cost function affects gradient size in shallow variational circuits.
gap: VQAs are heuristic methods whose scaling was unproven, and it was unclear whether shallow circuits would avoid vanishing gradients.
method: The authors prove two results for alternating layered ansatz circuits built from blocks forming local 2-designs, then illustrate them with quantum autoencoder simulations of up to 100 qubits.
results: Global observables produce exponentially vanishing gradients even at shallow depth. Local observables give at worst polynomially vanishing gradients when depth is logarithmic in the number of qubits, which links locality to trainability.
limits: The proofs hold for a specific class of ansatz, and they address trainability alone. A trainable cost function may still fail to give good accuracy on a real task.
technique: Barren plateau theory; local vs global cost
mm: Proofs for layered ansatz; 100-qubit autoencoder simulation
f: Global costs give barren plateaus; local costs stay trainable at log depth
